## The idea

A transcription begins with a musical source, but it also begins with a
decision about evidence. You need to know which score or recording you heard,
where to find it again, and what its stated terms allow you to do. Treating that
paperwork as something to reconstruct after the notes are entered creates
trouble when two editions disagree about a measure or the original page can no
longer be recovered for a shared arrangement.

Source libraries require different kinds of care. IMSLP contains scans and
editions whose legal status can vary by item and jurisdiction. Mutopia presents
typeset scores with terms displayed for each item. MuseScore contains community
uploads, so access to a page does not by itself settle the rights attached to
the upload. *Public domain* is a legal status, not another name for old music.
The underlying composition may be free of copyright while a recent engraving,
translation, performance, or arrangement remains protected.

The practical answer is a small source record kept beside the score data. Give
it the title, composer, edition or arranger, repository, stable page address,
displayed licence statement, access date, and the bars you plan to transcribe.
This record is not decoration around the musical work. It is the route back to
the evidence when a pitch, measure number, or permission later needs checking.

## Run this

This program keeps the source description and a first audition in the same
object. Its seven-note phrase is invented, which avoids making any claim about
a named edition while the fields are still placeholders. Notice that the
metadata can be incomplete without preventing playback. That is precisely why
the log prints the missing information where you cannot overlook it.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84
use_synth :piano

candidate = {
  title: "Practice candidate",
  repository: "replace with the source collection",
  licence: "copy the exact statement from the source page",
  accessed: "YYYY-MM-DD",
  bars: "1-4",
  notes: [:c4, :d4, :e4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :c4],
  durations: [0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 2]
}

candidate[:notes].zip(candidate[:durations]).each do |note_name, duration|
  play note_name, release: duration * 0.8
  sleep duration
end

puts "Source: #{candidate[:repository]}"
puts "Licence note: #{candidate[:licence]}"
```

The phrase rises from C to G and returns, ending with a long C that sounds
settled. At the same time, the log exposes the unfinished repository and
licence fields. The music can play, but the candidate is not yet ready to
become the basis of a shareable transcription. Keeping both facts visible
prevents a pleasant audition from quietly outrunning the source work.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the repository and licence strings with the wording from one real
   candidate page. Preserve that wording instead of paraphrasing it. Run the
   phrase again and read the log as if you had received it from someone else:
   could you recover the same page without asking which version they meant?
2. Replace the invented notes and durations with one complete phrase from a
   candidate whose stated terms fit your intended use. Keep the bar range with
   the data. Listen for the phrase ending rather than stopping merely because
   four measures have elapsed; a cut through a cadence will make the extract
   feel interrupted.
3. Add an edition or arranger field. If the page supplies neither, record
   `"not stated"`. Playback stays identical, which makes the lesson useful:
   provenance can improve even when no audible property changes.

## Why it works

Programmers are accustomed to values whose later treatment depends on
metadata. A file's bytes cannot tell you whether redistribution is permitted;
the same bytes can arrive under different terms. Pitches have the same
limitation. Two pages may encode the same composition while the scan,
engraving, editorial additions, or arrangement on each page has a different
status.

Provenance also improves musical debugging. Suppose measure 7 sounds wrong a
week after entry. With a source record, you can reopen the exact artefact and
compare the event against a stable coordinate. Without it, even the phrase
"measure 7" may be ambiguous: another edition may count a pickup differently,
renumber a section, or print a variant reading. The edition field explains why
two careful transcriptions can disagree.

A shortlist helps reveal these practical differences before you commit to a
long project. Twenty candidates is enough to compare range, texture, score
clarity, recording availability, and displayed terms. For a first ear
transcription, a clear monophonic line lets you hear individual attacks. For a
score-entry project, readable engraving and stable measure numbers reduce the
number of unrelated uncertainties. Musical ambition is easier to sustain when
the evidence itself is usable.

This workflow is not legal advice. Copyright duration and public-domain rules
depend on jurisdiction, and a composer's death date does not settle the status
of every edition or recording. When a page is unclear, choose a source with an
explicit statement or obtain advice suited to the place and manner in which
you intend to publish.

## Take it further

Create `sources.md` and describe twenty candidates. For each one, record a
stable page address, the displayed licence or public-domain statement, the date
you accessed it, the named edition or arranger, approximate difficulty,
texture, and a proposed bar range. Then reduce the list to three choices: one
melody for transcription by ear, one score for exact entry, and one larger
capstone candidate. Write the entries so another reader can recover every
source and understand why each extract is musically workable without having to
ask which version you meant.
